en.title: Martin Scorsese Blames Seth Rogen for Killing His 'Cleopatra' Epic
en.summary: A legendary director's passion project met an untimely end, and he's pointing the finger at a comedy duo. The fallout from a controversial 2014 film continues to ripple through Hollywood.
en.body:
In a candid revelation that will send ripples through cinephile circles, legendary director **Martin Scorsese** has revealed that his planned epic on the life of **Cleopatra** was ultimately scuttled due to the comedic actions of **Seth Rogen** and his 2014 film, *The Interview*. The film, a satirical take on a fictional assassination plot against North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, inadvertently triggered a chain of events that torpedoed Scorsese's decades-long ambition to bring the Egyptian queen to the big screen.

Scorsese shared this surprising detail during a conversation for the Tribeca Film Festival's YouTube channel. When asked about a film he wished he had made, the director initially mused about *Gladiator* and other historical epics before his daughter, Francesca, prompted him about a potential **Cleopatra** project. Scorsese explained that his vision for the film, which would have starred **Angelina Jolie**, was shelved following the 2014 Sony Pictures hack. This hack was a direct consequence of *The Interview*'s controversial premise, which deeply angered the North Korean regime. The ensuing data breach exposed sensitive studio information, and while Scorsese didn't explicitly state the hack directly canceled *Cleopatra*, he directly linked the film's demise to the fallout from Rogen's comedy.

> "They made fun of Kim Jong Il" in *The Interview*, Scorsese stated, referring to the film's satirical targets. While the film actually targeted Kim Jong Un, Scorsese's remark, even with the slight factual inaccuracy about the specific leader, underscores the direct causal link he perceives. The controversy surrounding *The Interview* led to widespread cyberattacks, including the leak of confidential emails and studio data, creating an environment of instability and risk aversion within Hollywood that likely made a massive, potentially controversial project like Scorsese's **Cleopatra** untenable.

## The Unforeseen Consequences of Satire

For fans who dream of seeing **Martin Scorsese** tackle the grandeur of ancient Egypt with his signature cinematic prowess, this news is a bitter pill. **Cleopatra** has long been a passion project for the director, and the idea of his lens on such a monumental historical figure, potentially alongside a star like **Angelina Jolie**, was a tantalizing prospect. The fact that this ambitious undertaking was allegedly felled not by creative differences or budget constraints, but by the geopolitical fallout from a comedy that poked fun at a dictator, is a stark reminder of the interconnectedness of entertainment and global politics. It highlights how artistic decisions, even those made in jest, can have profound and far-reaching consequences, silencing the potential for other, very different artistic visions.

## What's Next for Scorsese's Unmade Epics

While **Cleopatra** joins a list of tantalizing projects that never came to fruition in Scorsese's storied career, the director remains actively engaged in filmmaking. Fans can look forward to his continued exploration of complex characters and historical narratives in future endeavors. Details regarding his immediate upcoming projects have not yet been announced, but his commitment to compelling storytelling suggests more cinematic masterpieces are on the horizon, even if they aren't about ancient Egyptian rulers.

content_raw: Just as Seth Rogen’s character Matt Remnick dashed Martin Scorsese’s opportunity to direct his Jonestown Massacre epic, Kool-Aid , on Apple TV’s The Studio , the real Rogen has done his fair share of damage to the auteur’s directorial ambitions. In a new video for the Tribeca Film Festival’s YouTube page, Scorsese reveals he was set to direct Angelina Jolie in Cleopatra before Rogen and his movie The Interview screwed it all up.  In the video, Francesca asks her dad about a movie he wished he made. After searching his mind for an example (offering the very literal answer, “You can’t make what somebody [made], you know?”), someone off-screen suggests Gladiator . “I would’ve done it a little differently,” Scorsese says with a wink, “if I’d come up with a plot.” He rattles off a few ideas, such as Abel Ferrara’s Bad Lieutenant , before Francesca says, “I feel like you always wanted to make a big Roman epic. Weren’t you going to do Cleopatra ?” Indeed, he was.  Unfortunately, the director explains, his Cleopatra was canceled because “they made fun of Kim Jong Il” in the 2013 Seth Rogen comedy The Interview . It was Kim Jong Un, but he was closer than YouTube’s closed captions, which transcribed Scorsese’s mistake as “Kim John Hill.” Yup, Scorsese’s Cleopatra was a victim of the Sony hack.  For those who don’t remember, in 2014, ahead of the release of The Interview , a comedy about a foolish cable news host looking to land an interview with Kim Jong Un, the North Korean government leaked a trove of emails from Sony executives’ work inboxes. The leaks revealed secret movie information, such as what’s going on with Spider-Man and how sorry George Clooney was about Monuments Men . The hack was a major embarrassment for the studio, which eventually dumped The Interview onto Netflix and set us on a course for the present day. But in Scorsese’s recollection: “[Kim Jong Un] got mad and he blew up everyone. We were going to do it. Eric Roth was already on the script. It was Angelina Jolie. We were going. She was Cleopatra VII. It was going to be really wild.” Visibly upset by the news, Francesca bemoans the movie that never was. Scorsese continues, “Well, tell Seth because they ruined everything just because Kim Jong Un doesn’t have a sense of humor.”  Since 1963’s Joseph L. Mankiewicz-directed Cleopatra , starring Elizabeth Taylor, became one of the biggest fiascoes in Hollywood history, famous directors have vied for the chance to break the curse. Scorsese won an early 2010s bake-off to direct a Scott Rudin-produced version based on the biography Cleopatra: A Life , with Jolie on the throne. Other names circling the production included David Fincher, Paul Greengrass , Ang Lee, and James Cameron, who wanted to do it in 3-D, natch.
